## Repositories, archives and registries {#open-research-infrastructures .smaller}

::: {.small}
| Kind | What it does | Examples |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Data archive** | holds survey data under the terms of their owners, often behind a registration and a licence | GESIS, the UK Data Service, ICPSR |
| **Statistical office** | publishes official series, usually open for reuse with attribution | Eurostat, the World Bank, national offices |
| **Repository** | keeps data, code and documents at a permanent address that can be cited | the OSF, Zenodo, Dataverse |
| **Registry** | files a dated plan that nobody can edit afterwards | OSF Registries, AsPredicted |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Each answers a question that a reader of a paper asks: where the data are and on what terms, where the code is, and what the authors planned before they had a result.
:::

::: notes
The practices of open research need places to live, and four kinds of infrastructure carry most of them. Data archives hold survey data on behalf of the people who collected them, often behind a registration and a licence, and GESIS, which holds the Eurobarometer, is one. Statistical offices publish the official series, such as unemployment, usually under an open licence that asks only for attribution. Repositories keep data, code and documents at a permanent address that can be cited, and the OSF is the one that this case lives on. Registries file a plan with a date on it, so that a reader can check what was intended before the result arrived. [advance] Each of the four answers a question that a careful reader of a paper asks, and the case of the day touches all four.
:::

## The data of the case and their terms {#the-data-of-the-case-and-their-terms .smaller}

::: {.small}
| What | Where | Terms |
|:--|:--|:--|
| The sixteen Eurobarometer waves, 2004–2013 | GESIS | free registration; no redistribution, no publication of individual cases, no processing by AI systems |
| Unemployment and GDP growth | the World Bank and Eurostat | open, with attribution |
| The country-year panel and the two analyst files of the course | the course site, and the panel also on the OSF | aggregates only, CC BY 4.0 |
| The results of the five analysts | the Multi100 data on the OSF | public |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The terms decide what a reproduction can use. Three of the five analyses rest on country means and reproduce in your browser; the other two rest on respondents, whose files each person downloads from GESIS under an account of their own.
:::

::: notes
Here is where every piece of today's data comes from, and on what terms. The respondents are in sixteen Eurobarometer waves held by GESIS: registration is free, but the terms forbid passing the files on, publishing individual cases or processing them with AI systems. The unemployment and growth series come from the World Bank and Eurostat, open to anyone who credits the source. The panel that we work on, and the two files that the course rebuilt for two of the analysts, are means of several hundred respondents or more per cell, which the terms allow to be published. [advance] This is why the licence is part of reproducibility. The three analyses that work on country means reproduce in your browser today, while the two that work on respondents need the GESIS files, and those can only reach you through your own account.
:::
